IPV-10-native.title: Perfect unison (P1) on the keyboard
IPV-10-native.desc: A piano keyboard from C4 to C5 with C4 highlighted (both notes are the same key). Perfect unison, P1: 0 semitones, counted as 0 one-key hops.

IPV-11-native.title: Minor second (m2) on the keyboard
IPV-11-native.desc: A piano keyboard from C4 to C5 with C4 and D♭4 highlighted. Minor second, m2: 1 semitones, counted as 1 one-key hops.

IPV-12-native.title: Major second (M2) on the keyboard
IPV-12-native.desc: A piano keyboard from C4 to C5 with C4 and D4 highlighted. Major second, M2: 2 semitones, counted as 2 one-key hops.

IPV-13-native.title: Minor third (m3) on the keyboard
IPV-13-native.desc: A piano keyboard from C4 to C5 with C4 and E♭4 highlighted. Minor third, m3: 3 semitones, counted as 3 one-key hops.

IPV-14-native.title: Major third (M3) on the keyboard
IPV-14-native.desc: A piano keyboard from C4 to C5 with C4 and E4 highlighted. Major third, M3: 4 semitones, counted as 4 one-key hops.

IPV-15-native.title: Perfect fourth (P4) on the keyboard
IPV-15-native.desc: A piano keyboard from C4 to C5 with C4 and F4 highlighted. Perfect fourth, P4: 5 semitones, counted as 5 one-key hops.

IPV-16-native.title: Tritone (A4/d5) on the keyboard
IPV-16-native.desc: A piano keyboard from C4 to C5 with C4 and F♯4 highlighted. Tritone, A4/d5: 6 semitones, counted as 6 one-key hops; the same key can also be written G♭4 as a diminished fifth.

IPV-17-native.title: Perfect fifth (P5) on the keyboard
IPV-17-native.desc: A piano keyboard from C4 to C5 with C4 and G4 highlighted. Perfect fifth, P5: 7 semitones, counted as 7 one-key hops.

IPV-18-native.title: Minor sixth (m6) on the keyboard
IPV-18-native.desc: A piano keyboard from C4 to C5 with C4 and A♭4 highlighted. Minor sixth, m6: 8 semitones, counted as 8 one-key hops.

IPV-19-native.title: Major sixth (M6) on the keyboard
IPV-19-native.desc: A piano keyboard from C4 to C5 with C4 and A4 highlighted. Major sixth, M6: 9 semitones, counted as 9 one-key hops.

IPV-20-native.title: Minor seventh (m7) on the keyboard
IPV-20-native.desc: A piano keyboard from C4 to C5 with C4 and B♭4 highlighted. Minor seventh, m7: 10 semitones, counted as 10 one-key hops.

IPV-21-native.title: Major seventh (M7) on the keyboard
IPV-21-native.desc: A piano keyboard from C4 to C5 with C4 and B4 highlighted. Major seventh, M7: 11 semitones, counted as 11 one-key hops.

IPV-22-native.title: Perfect octave (P8) on the keyboard
IPV-22-native.desc: A piano keyboard from C4 to C5 with C4 and C5 highlighted. Perfect octave, P8: 12 semitones, counted as 12 one-key hops.

IPV-04-native.title: Interval example: C4 to E4
IPV-04-native.desc: A keyboard from C4 to C5 with C4 and E4 highlighted and four numbered semitone hops between them: C to C-sharp, to D, to D-sharp, to E. The distance, four semitones, is the interval.
IPV-04-native.teach: Interval = distance between two pitches; worked example C4→E4 = 4 semitones.

IPV-05-native.title: The same two notes, melodic and harmonic
IPV-05-native.desc: Two time strips for the same notes, C4 and E4. In the first strip C4 sounds during seconds 0 to 2 and then E4 during seconds 2 to 4, one after another. In the second both notes last the whole 4 seconds, together. The distance is four semitones in both.
IPV-05-native.teach: Same two notes, played one after another (melodic) or together (harmonic).

IPV-06-native.title: Reading the keyboard: white-key neighbours are not always one semitone
IPV-06-native.desc: A keyboard from C4 to C5 showing black keys in groups of two then three. C to D spans two semitones because C-sharp sits between them. E to F spans only one semitone because there is no black key between E and F.
IPV-06-native.teach: Letter names vs semitones; two-then-three black keys; C→D = 2 semitones, E→F = 1.

IPV-07-native.title: Thirteen intervals on a 0 to 12 semitone ruler
IPV-07-native.desc: A ruler from 0 to 12 semitones above C4 with thirteen marked landmarks in order: P1, m2, M2, m3, M3, P4, A4 or d5, P5, m6, M6, m7, M7, P8. The ruler shows measured distance only.
IPV-07-native.teach: Increasing measured distance, 0–12 semitones; not an order of tension.

IPV-30-native.title: The thirteen interval landmarks with note pairs
IPV-30-native.desc: A 0 to 12 semitone ruler with each landmark named and paired with its notes above C4, from the perfect unison C to C through the tritone C to F-sharp or G-flat up to the perfect octave C to C. Positions are exact semitone counts.
IPV-30-native.teach: The thirteen landmarks with names and note pairs, exact positions.

IPV-30-narrow.title: Thirteen interval landmarks (list)
IPV-30-narrow.desc: The thirteen intervals from 0 to 12 semitones above C4, listed with abbreviation, name and note pair.
IPV-30-narrow.teach: Narrow vertical list of the thirteen landmarks for phones.

IPV-23-native.title: Minor second compared with Major second
IPV-23-native.desc: Two keyboards, each from C4 to C5. The first highlights C4 and D♭4, 1 semitone. The second highlights C4 and D4, 2 semitones. The lower note C4 stays; the upper note moves one key.

IPV-24-native.title: Minor third compared with Major third
IPV-24-native.desc: Two keyboards, each from C4 to C5. The first highlights C4 and E♭4, 3 semitones. The second highlights C4 and E4, 4 semitones. The lower note C4 stays; the upper note moves one key.

IPV-26-native.title: Minor sixth compared with Major sixth
IPV-26-native.desc: Two keyboards, each from C4 to C5. The first highlights C4 and A♭4, 8 semitones. The second highlights C4 and A4, 9 semitones. The lower note C4 stays; the upper note moves one key.

IPV-27-native.title: Minor seventh compared with Major seventh
IPV-27-native.desc: Two keyboards, each from C4 to C5. The first highlights C4 and B♭4, 10 semitones. The second highlights C4 and B4, 11 semitones. The lower note C4 stays; the upper note moves one key.

IPV-09-native.title: Perfect fourth compared with Perfect fifth
IPV-09-native.desc: Two keyboards, each from C4 to C5. The first highlights C4 and F4, 5 semitones. The second highlights C4 and G4, 7 semitones. The lower note C4 stays; the upper note moves one key.

IPV-25-native.title: Perfect fourth, tritone and perfect fifth
IPV-25-native.desc: Three keyboards from C4 to C5 with C4 as the shared lower note and the upper note at F4 (5 semitones, perfect fourth), F-sharp4 (6 semitones, tritone, also written G-flat4) and G4 (7 semitones, perfect fifth).
IPV-25-native.teach: Five, six, seven semitones; tritone spelling.

IPV-28-native.title: The same interval in three registers
IPV-28-native.desc: Three keyboards showing the same perfect fifth, 7 semitones, built from C in a low, a middle and a high register. The distance is identical; the sound you get depends on register and instrument.
IPV-28-native.teach: One interval, three registers; no universal consonance scale.

IPV-29-native.title: Inversion: moving the lower note up an octave
IPV-29-native.desc: Three pairs. Take the lower note and move it up an octave. A minor third of 3 semitones (C to E-flat) becomes a major sixth of 9 (E-flat to C). A major third of 4 becomes a minor sixth of 8. A perfect fourth of 5 becomes a perfect fifth of 7. Each pair adds to 12 semitones; the interval numbers add to 9.
IPV-29-native.teach: Inversion pairs m3↔M6, M3↔m6, P4↔P5: semitones add to 12.

IPV-34-native.title: Same key, two interval names
IPV-34-native.desc: Two keyboards with the same two keys highlighted, C4 and the black key above D. First it is spelled E-flat: letters C, D, E make a third, so it is a minor third. Second it is spelled D-sharp: letters C, D make a second, so it is an augmented second. Both are 3 semitones.
IPV-34-native.teach: An interval name comes from letter distance as well as semitones: same key, two spellings.

IPV-35-native.title: Adding a third note changes the whole sound-world
IPV-35-native.desc: Three keyboards from C4. First C and E alone, a major third of 4 semitones. Second C, E and G together, a C-major triad. Third C, E-flat and G, a C-minor triad, where moving one key down changes the quality.
IPV-35-native.teach: Adding a third note changes the world: dyad C–E versus C–E–G versus C–E♭–G.
